heading_path: Buyer's Guide Determine the procurement strategy - Developing a procurement strategy
blocks.markdown: Developing a procurement strategy The development of the procurement strategy begins with initial discussions between you as the buyer and the client. It is the most important step in the procurement process, as it influences the scope of the requirement and determines the level of competition. You must consider the Public Services and Procurement Canada’s ( PSPC ) Guiding principles when developing a procurement strategy. Meeting operational and legal requirements Ensure the procurement strategy satisfies the client's operational requirements. Make sure it also complies with legal requirements, while achieving best value, and advancing national objectives. Conducting complete pricing and risk assessment Assess pricing considerations, options and potential risks early on and throughout the acquisition lifecycle. Align the pricing strategy to the procurement strategy. Refer to sections 1, 2 and 3 of the Practitioner’s Guide for Procurement Pricing for more information. Providing a challenge function To maintain the integrity of the procurement process, you should provide a challenge function during the procurement strategy stage. This function helps ensure transparency and fairness. Examples of applying this function include: advocating for early engagement with industry when possible challenging any proposed non-competitive procurements to ensure the justification is well-supported and can withstand public scrutiny ensuring specific requirements aren't overly restrictive, which could unnecessarily limit competition confirming the appropriate solicitation method is used using advanced contract award notices only when suitable documenting all decisions related to dividing or unbundling a requirement into smaller parts, ensuring these decisions aren't intended to bypass financial approval thresholds or policy requirements, such as contract entry limits or trade agreement obligations Considerations for the procurement strategy In developing the most effective procurement strategy, you and the client must consider a few factors. If applicable, you must: choose the most suitable method of supply for the procurement assess the total estimated cost, including all options, maintenance, and storage costs, ensuring a comprehensive understanding of the financial implications of the entire lifecycle cost of the procurement determine the contract period, including any options for extension consider delivery requirements, including specific delivery timelines or milestones plan the procurement schedule, detailing the procurement activities can help the project stay on time establish evaluation procedures and a method of selection, detailing the criteria for evaluating offers and selecting the supplier consider the environmental impact of procurement decisions weigh the benefits of procuring commercial (off-the-shelf products) products against customized solutions identify potential risks associated with the procurement and mitigation strategies set clear terms for liability and indemnification decide on the involvement of a fairness monitor to ensure the integrity of the procurement process allow small and medium enterprises to participate incorporate opportunities for Indigenous businesses ensure the procurement meets accessibility standards align the procurement with broader government national objectives ensure new procurements are compatible with existing systems or solutions look for opportunities to consolidate procurements for efficiency and cost savings consider the end-of-life disposal of the product plan for the renewal or replacement of goods or services, including all transfer costs Approval process You must give the approval authority the opportunity to approve or reject the proposed procurement strategy as early as possible in the process. Preventing them from investing significant effort and time in a strategy that may not be approved. The procurement strategy must identify any deviations to contracting policies. Learn more about how to Prepare approval documents . Note : To ensure alignment with original objectives and compliance with policy, you must seek re-approval for any major changes to the procurement strategy during the process.

heading_path: Buyer's Guide Determine the procurement strategy - Developing a procurement strategy
blocks.markdown:
- choose the most suitable method of supply for the procurement
- assess the total estimated cost, including all options, maintenance, and storage costs, ensuring a comprehensive understanding of the financial implications of the entire lifecycle cost of the procurement
- determine the contract period, including any options for extension
- consider delivery requirements, including specific delivery timelines or milestones
- plan the procurement schedule, detailing the procurement activities can help the project stay on time
- establish evaluation procedures and a method of selection, detailing the criteria for evaluating offers and selecting the supplier
- consider the environmental impact of procurement decisions
- weigh the benefits of procuring commercial (off-the-shelf products) products against customized solutions
- identify potential risks associated with the procurement and mitigation strategies
- set clear terms for liability and indemnification
- decide on the involvement of a fairness monitor to ensure the integrity of the procurement process
- allow small and medium enterprises to participate
- incorporate opportunities for Indigenous businesses
- ensure the procurement meets accessibility standards
- align the procurement with broader government national objectives
- ensure new procurements are compatible with existing systems or solutions
- look for opportunities to consolidate procurements for efficiency and cost savings
- consider the end-of-life disposal of the product
- plan for the renewal or replacement of goods or services, including all transfer costs
